query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non‐equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA (density <6 g/cm³) initially produced by rapid solidification, controlled thermal exposure (aging/heat treatment) promotes the diffusion‐mediated precipitation of fine, Mg-rich intermetallic compounds from the dominant supersaturated solid-solution matrix. These newly formed intermetallic particles act as structural mediators that locally modify the electrochemical potential and serve as nucleation sites for passivating oxide formation. As a consequence, the alloy’s high-temperature oxidation behavior shifts toward the formation of a more continuous, protective oxide film (for example, enriched in Ti/Cu oxides or mixed Mg-oxides) and its corrosion response in aggressive media is improved relative to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast lightweight high-entropy alloy containing Mg, with a predominantly single-phase (metastable) solid solution and a minor content of randomly distributed intermetallics.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal aging (heat treatment) regimen designed to trigger diffusion-driven partitioning and nucleation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
generation.conditions: Experimental comparison at ambient and high-temperature environments (corrosion in chloride solution and oxidation at elevated temperatures, e.g., 600–800 °C) with alloys maintaining overall density below 6 g/cm³ and similar base composition.
generation.structural_mediator: Fine-scale, precipitated Mg-rich intermetallic compounds that segregate from the matrix and promote the formation and adherence of passivating surface oxides.
generation.mechanism: During post-casting heat treatment, Mg (and possibly other reactive elements such as Cu or Gd) diffuses within the matrix, yielding a refined dispersion of intermetallic compounds. These precipitates create local differences in electrochemical potential that facilitate the preferential formation of a protective surface film during oxidation. This passivation layer not only retards aggressive ionic attack (thereby altering corrosion behavior) but also enhances the high-temperature oxidation resistance by limiting oxygen ingress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, heat-treated samples will exhibit a more uniform, fine-scale distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic phases, accompanied by the development of a denser and compositionally modified oxide scale. In corrosion testing (e.g., in 0.1 M NaCl), such samples should demonstrate lower corrosion current densities and more positive corrosion potentials. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the aged samples are expected to show reduced oxidation weight gain and a more coherent, protective oxide morphology.
generation.baseline: The initial non-equilibrium as-cast microstructure with a largely supersaturated solid-solution and only coarse or minimal intermetallic formation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Mg-containing lightweight HEAs with densities below 6 g/cm³ and similar alloying designs; deviations in the elemental ratios (especially of reactive elements like Cu, Gd, or Ti) or processing conditions that yield a very different as-cast microstructure could lead to different transformation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The proposed mechanism builds upon the observed non-equilibrium phase evolution in lightweight complex concentrated alloys (see PMC7579168::web::035::5_conclusions and PMC9100001::web::000::abstract) and the role of passivating surface films in Mg-containing systems for improved corrosion resistance (see PMC12299034::web::007::1_introduction). What is new here is the explicit linking of heat-treatment induced precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallics as a mediator for both enhanced oxide scale formation during high-temperature oxidation and improved corrosion behavior. However, the exact identity and distribution of the intermetallic phases and oxide film compositions remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with identical composition and casting parameters. One set is retained in the as-cast state; the other undergoes a controlled heat treatment designed to trigger intermetallic precipitation (e.g., annealing at a sub-solidus temperature for a specified duration). Use high-resolution microscopy (TEM/SEM with EDS) to characterize the microstructure, with particular attention to the size and uniformity of the precipitated Mg-rich intermetallic phases. Subsequently, conduct corrosion tests (potentiodynamic polarization in 0.1 M NaCl) and high-temperature oxidation experiments (exposure at 600–800 °C with weight gain and surface oxide characterization via XPS or Raman spectroscopy).
measurements: Quantitative microstructural analysis (size, distribution, and phase identification of intermetallics) via TEM/SEM
Potentiodynamic polarization curves and corrosion current densities
Oxidation weight gain measurements and oxide scale morphology/composition (using XPS, Raman, or similar techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If heat-treated samples do not show a significant refinement or increase in the volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallic phases compared to the as-cast samples, or if no measurable improvement (i.e., lower corrosion current density, more positive corrosion potential, and reduced oxidation weight gain with enhanced oxide film quality) is observed relative to the as-cast baseline, then the hypothesis that the intermetallic evolution mediates improved corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The aim of the present work is to investigate the influence of systematic variations in Mg content on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion behavior of these alloys. By characterizing the resulting intermetallic phases, grain refinement, and passive film formation, this study identified how processing and composition synergistically affect the corrosion resistance and mechanical performance. This work offers new insights into the design of corrosion-resistant, high-strength materials and represents a novel extension of compositionally complex alloy design to Mg-rich systems.

Intermetallic compound-based phases were found at lower concentrations but still significantly higher than in the conventional aluminum alloys. Two invariant transformations were indicated for Al3.4Cu0.5Si0.2Zn0.5Mg0.2 alloy, with a BCC-A2 phase stable between 316–488 °C. AbstractIn the current work, a novel complex concentrated aluminum alloy is designed and studied. In order to investigate the unknown region of the multicomponent phase diagrams, thermo-physical parameters and the CALPHAD method were used to understand the phase formation of the Al58Mg18Zn12Cu5Si7 at.% (Al47.4Mg13.3Zn23.8Cu9.6Si6wt.%) alloy with a low-density of 2.63 g/cm3. The CALPHAD methodology showed good agreement with both the investigated microstructure and the thermodynamic parameters. The designed alloy was manufactured using an induction furnace and pour mold casting process. This study avoids the use of expensive, dangerous or scarce alloying elements and focuses instead on the utilization of widely available relatively cheaper elements. The microstructural evolution as a function of the heat-treatment was studied by means of different microstructural characterization techniques. The hardness, compressive strength and electrical conductivity of the as-cast and heat-treated alloy at room temperature were studied and correlated with the previously characterized microstructure.
